_about: Prepared defences (the grand campaign). An army that spends a whole month where it stands, without marching or fighting, digs in whoever commands it, the computer's armies as well as the player's. Against troops who are dug in and in supply the day's luck runs against the attacker, so that odds which would be safe in the open become a gamble, and an attack thrown back from such a line has shot its bolt for the month. Rules in src/campaign/game.ts (assess, resolveBattle, endPhase).

notes.entrench: 'auto': every corps in the field that ends its own month having neither moved nor fought is dug in from then on, unless it is under orders to give ground. Troops inside a town are not: its walls are their works. A corps that leaves the ground leaves its fieldworks behind it (players read 'fieldworks', never 'trenches': Brian, 2026-11-14). With 'auto' off only the player's corps under orders to dig do so, as in the historical scenarios. 'months': how long the works take to finish. A corps counts toward a prepared defence by what its works are worth so far: 'share' gives that for one month's digging, two and three, since the first month's work does the most.
notes.handover: Hand over the fieldworks (Version 64). Works belong to the ground. A dug-in corps that marches off, entrains or goes forward after a battle won leaves its positions behind: a corps of its own side standing there without works takes them over at once, and otherwise they wait for the next corps of that side to march or ride in, which has them, as old as they were, from the moment it arrives and keeps them at the month's end though it marched. Standing empty they lose 'fade' months of work at the start of each of their owner's months, and they are gone the moment the enemy sets foot there. Troops driven off their ground leave nothing, and troops falling back or put down by any other means take nothing over. Remove the key to have works lost when a corps leaves, as before Version 64.
notes.probe: Probe the line (Version 64). One fighting corps of the player's feels out the enemy army in the province beside it: every corps there is identified as a battle would identify it, and the works of each one that is dug in lose 'wear' months, whatever the weight of the corps that probes. It costs the probing corps 'loss' of its men, 'org' of its organisation and 'ap' of its moves, and it counts as having fought, so it does no digging that month. The defenders lose no men; they count as attacked, so they dig at the pace of troops who were. Nothing changes hands, no battle is filed, no offensive is opened by it, and a line is probed once a month at most. No computer staff probes.
notes.prepared: 'dice' is the run of the day's luck for an attack on defenders who are all dug in and in supply (in the open it is 0.8 to 1.2, and it takes 1.2 to 1 on the day to carry the ground). Where only part of the defence is prepared the run lies between the two in proportion, and massed guns in the attack take their share off it as they do off the fieldworks. 'spentAt': an attack that fails against a defence at least this far prepared leaves the attacking corps with no moves for the rest of the month. 'surprise': how much of its preparedness a line loses to a new offensive by an army trained to it (Germany's): for 'surpriseMonths' months from its first blow, or for 'openingMonths' if it is the first offensive that army has ever made on that country. 'armour': how much it loses to an attack with tanks in it when the defence has no armour of its own. Both multiply with what the guns take off. 'losses': against a fully prepared line the attackers lose 'attacker' times the men they would in the open and the defenders 'defender' times, in proportion where the line is partly prepared.
notes.wear: Works wear down under attack (Version 61). Every attack on dug-in troops, won or lost, takes 'perAttack' months off the works of each defender who stays, in full if the attack came at 'fullAt' to 1 or better on the Battle Ticket and in proportion below that, so that a jab by one corps scratches a line and a real blow breaks into it. Massed guns in the attack add to it: by 'guns' times the share they take off the fieldworks. Works are never worn below nothing, and troops whose works are worn under one month lose the fieldworks' 25% in the same proportion. 'regrow': the months of digging a corps gets done in a month in which it was attacked. At a half, a line attacked once a month loses half a month's works every month and one attacked twice a month a month and a half, so steady pressure wears a line away and a quiet front builds it back. (At 0 the German player following history held Berlin to the end of 1944 in 17 to 19 wars of 24 instead of 12, and Moscow fell in 7 computer wars of 24 instead of 2: armies in contact never dug at all.)
notes.tired: Defenders who have already fought this month fight the next blow tired (Version 63). Every attack a corps stands against in the field, won or lost, counts against it until its own month begins again: 'per' off its defence for each blow at full weight, up to 'most' blows. The weight of a blow is the same measure the wear on works uses: full at wear.fullAt to 1 or better on the Battle Ticket, in proportion below that. The defenders' losses in men and in organisation go by the same weight, so that a jab by one corps at a great stack costs it almost nothing and tires nobody.
notes.hammer: The computer's two-wave attack (Version 63). Where its whole force cannot carry a place at the odds its staff asks, it sends a first wave to wear the works and tire the defence and the main body after it in the same month: the first wave must come at 'first' to 1 or better, and the main body must then have the staff's usual odds times 'second'. A slow command plans it too, since it is one operation laid on beforehand.
notes.frontage: Attacked from 'sides' provinces or more at once, a defence cannot cover every road: each side's roads carry 'extra' more corps. Against fortress works or dug-in troops up to 'guns' artillery corps join an attack without taking room on the roads, since they fire over the heads of the infantry.
notes.staff: 'odds': how much better odds than usual a computer staff asks before it attacks a fully prepared line. At 0 it attacks as it always did, and learns the cost in men.
notes.measured: Over 72 computer wars to the end of 1944 (Version 57 before, Version 58 after): Berlin fallen in 38 and 25, the German army still deep in Russia in 16 and 7, neither in 10 and 40; Paris falls between 2 and 3 months later. Of 36 wars run on to January 1947 Berlin had fallen in 29 and 7 were undecided. A dug-in, supplied line now throws back an attack at 1.5 to 1 about 4 times in 10 and at 2 to 1 about 1 in 7; nothing is safe under 2.4 to 1. Version 61 (works that wear, the share of each month's digging, the opening offensive, room on the roads), over 24 computer wars to December 1944 against Version 60: Paris falls in October 1940 at the median (November) and by August in 5 (none), Berlin has fallen in 6 (5) and Moscow in 4 (2); finished, supplied lines throw back 60% of attacks at 1.2 to 1.6 to 1 and 26% at 1.6 to 2.2 to 1 (59% and 23%); 280 attacks thrown back wore works down. Over 24 wars played as Germany on history's plan at Colonel, Berlin holds to the end of 1944 in 13 (12). A Soviet player who strikes first in June 1940 takes Berlin from Germany in 6 wars of 8 (4).
